metadata.note: Teaching assistants except postsecondary 1.42M (BLS May 2025). Distinct from the Teaching bank, which covers lead teachers. Covers safeguarding and disclosure handling, supporting without creating dependence, individual education plans and legally required provision, behaviour plans and de-escalation, small group intervention delivery, confidentiality and parent boundaries, and the deployment and inclusion leadership track.

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and your experience working with students.

key_points: Setting and age range first: elementary, middle, high school, or early years. Then general classroom, special education, or one to one support
Say the support type: whole class support, small group instruction, one to one for a specific student, behaviour support, or personal care
Numbers: class sizes, how many students you supported, how many teachers you worked with, hours per week
Training and clearances: background check, first aid, any behaviour or crisis intervention training, paraprofessional certification or assessment where the district requires it
One outcome: a student who progressed, a behaviour plan that worked, a routine you helped establish
Say why you want to support rather than lead a classroom, since that is a genuine question
strong_answer_signals: Names the age range and the support type
Clearances and training stated without being asked
Has a specific student outcome to point at
avoid: Describing the role as helping out in a classroom
Being vague about background checks or certification
Framing it as a step towards being a teacher without saying you value this role

questions.text: Tell me about a time you helped a student who was struggling.

key_points: Situation: what the student was struggling with. Be specific about the barrier: reading fluency, a maths concept, focus, anxiety, language, or a physical need
Action: how you broke it down. Smaller steps, a different explanation, a visual, a manipulative, extra practice, or simply time and patience
Say how you kept it dignified. Support that singles a student out publicly does more harm than good
Say how you communicated with the teacher about what worked
Result: the specific progress, and how the student felt about it
Anonymise the student properly
strong_answer_signals: Names the actual barrier rather than saying they were behind
Protects the student dignity
Feeds back to the teacher
avoid: Doing the work for the student
Identifying a student in a recognisable way
A story where you supported without the teacher knowing what you did

questions.text: Tell me about a challenging behaviour you handled.

key_points: Describe the behaviour, not the child. Refusal, disruption, leaving the room, aggression, shutting down, or distress
Action: stay calm and low key, reduce the audience, use the agreed strategy from the plan rather than improvising
Look for the function behind it: escape from a hard task, attention, sensory need, hunger, tiredness, or something happening at home
Follow the behaviour plan and the school policy exactly, especially on any physical intervention
Result: the student regulated, the lesson continued, and what you told the teacher afterwards
Say what you changed to prevent the next one
strong_answer_signals: Looks for the function behind the behaviour
Follows the plan rather than improvising
Reduces the audience rather than escalating
avoid: Any physical handling outside trained policy
Describing a child as a problem
Winning a confrontation in front of the class

questions.text: Tell me about working with a teacher.

key_points: Say what a good working relationship looks like: knowing the lesson plan in advance, agreeing your role, and a quick check in before and after
Action: how you learned their style and expectations, and how you asked without interrupting a lesson
Give an example of anticipating: preparing a resource, spotting a student about to struggle, adjusting a task without being asked
Result: the lesson ran better and the teacher relied on you
Say how you handled a disagreement about approach, privately and professionally
strong_answer_signals: Agrees the role in advance rather than guessing
Anticipates rather than waits
Raises disagreements privately
avoid: Contradicting a teacher in front of students
Waiting to be told what to do every lesson
A story that is mostly about a difficult teacher

questions.text: Tell me about a time you supported a student with additional needs.

key_points: Say the need in general terms and the support: autism, ADHD, dyslexia, speech and language, physical disability, hearing or vision, social and emotional needs
Action: follow the individual plan and the targets in it, and use the strategies agreed rather than your own invention
Say how you promoted independence rather than dependence, since that is the professional line in this work
Say how you handled personal care or medical needs if relevant, with dignity and to the agreed protocol
Result: the specific progress against a target
Say how you recorded and reported it
strong_answer_signals: Follows the individual plan and its targets
Promotes independence, not dependence
Records progress against targets
avoid: Creating your own approach outside the plan
Doing everything for the student
Discussing a student needs where others can hear

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to be flexible.

key_points: This job changes hour to hour: a cover class, a different student, a trip, a lesson that goes differently, a staff absence
Action: how you adapted without losing the students. Ask what is needed, take the task, and keep the routine steady for the children
Say how you handle being moved to an unfamiliar class or age group
Result: the day covered and the students settled
Say what you do when you are given no notice and no information
strong_answer_signals: Adapts without complaint and asks what is needed
Keeps routine steady for the students
Handles unfamiliar classes
avoid: Rigidity about your assigned student or class
Complaining about being moved
Leaving students unsettled during a change

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had a concern about a student.

key_points: This is a safeguarding question. Treat it as the most serious one in the interview
Say the type of concern in general terms: a disclosure, an injury, neglect signs, a change in behaviour, something a child said
Action: listen without leading or promising confidentiality, reassure, write it down in the child words as soon as possible
Report immediately to the designated safeguarding lead. It is not your job to investigate or to decide whether it is serious enough
Result: the referral made and the record kept
Say plainly that you never promise a child you will keep a secret
strong_answer_signals: Reports to the safeguarding lead immediately
Never promises confidentiality to a child
Records in the child own words
avoid: Deciding it was probably nothing
Investigating it yourself
Promising a child you will not tell anyone

questions.text: Tell me about a time you received feedback.

key_points: Real feedback here: prompting too much, stepping in too quickly, being too quiet, not following the behaviour plan consistently, missing a recording deadline
Action: how you asked what good looked like and what you changed
Result: the observable difference for the student
Say whether you asked the teacher to watch and give you more feedback afterwards
strong_answer_signals: Asks what good looks like
Change measured by student outcome
Invites more feedback
avoid: Feedback that was really praise
Explaining why the feedback was unfair
No change afterwards

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked with a parent or carer.

key_points: Be clear about the boundary first: what a teaching assistant can share is usually limited and routed through the teacher
Situation: a handover at the door, a question about the day, a concern raised informally
Action: be warm and factual about the routine, and direct anything about progress, behaviour or concerns to the teacher
Never discuss another child, and never share your own opinion about a diagnosis or a family situation
Result: the parent felt heard and the right person handled it
Say that you report anything a parent tells you that raises a concern
strong_answer_signals: Knows the boundary on what to share
Directs to the teacher rather than answering
Reports concerns raised informally
avoid: Discussing progress or behaviour without the teacher
Mentioning another child
Offering an opinion on a diagnosis

questions.text: Tell me about a time you helped a whole class, not just one student.

key_points: Examples: managing a group activity, supervising a transition, preparing resources, running a small group intervention, covering while the teacher dealt with an incident
Action: what you actually did and how you kept the learning going rather than just supervising
Say how you used the teacher plan rather than improvising
Result: the lesson continued, the group finished the task, the transition was calm
Say what you learned about managing more than one student at once
strong_answer_signals: Keeps learning going rather than only supervising
Works from the teacher plan
Handles transitions, which are where most classrooms lose time
avoid: Only ever describing one to one work
Improvising a lesson with no reference to the plan
Treating whole class moments as crowd control

questions.text: What do you understand about safeguarding and child protection?

key_points: Say the core principle: safeguarding is everyone responsibility and the child comes first, always
Know the signs across categories: physical, emotional, neglect, sexual abuse, and online harm
If a child discloses: listen, do not lead or ask probing questions, do not promise confidentiality, reassure them they did the right thing, record in their words, report immediately
Know who the designated safeguarding lead is in any school you work in, on day one
Report low level concerns too. A pattern is built from small observations
Professional conduct: never be alone with a child in a way that breaches policy, never share personal contact details, no social media contact
Say that you would report a concern about a colleague through the same route
strong_answer_signals: Reports without deciding whether it is serious enough
Never promises confidentiality
Would report a concern about a colleague
avoid: Investigating a disclosure
Asking a child leading questions
Not knowing who the safeguarding lead is

questions.text: How do you support learning without doing the work for the student?

key_points: Name the risk directly: over prompting creates dependence and hides what a student can actually do
Use a ladder of support: wait time first, then a prompt to think, then a question, then a hint, then a model. Give the least support that works
Wait longer than feels comfortable. Most adults intervene within three seconds and the student never gets there
Let the student struggle productively. Difficulty is where learning happens and rescuing removes it
Fade support deliberately over time and record what level of prompting was needed
Report honestly what the student did independently, since the teacher assessment depends on it
strong_answer_signals: Names dependence as the risk
Uses least support that works and fades it
Reports honestly what was independent
avoid: Giving the answer to keep the student moving
Sitting so close the student never attempts alone
Reporting work as independent when it was heavily prompted

questions.text: What behaviour management strategies do you use?

key_points: Prevention first: clear routines, knowing the triggers, preparing the student for change, and catching the good behaviour before the bad
Follow the school policy and the individual plan consistently. Inconsistency between adults is what breaks behaviour systems
Use low key responses first: proximity, a look, a quiet reminder, a redirection. Escalating early escalates the student
Give take up time after an instruction rather than standing over a student waiting
De-escalation: calm voice, reduce the audience, give choices, allow a way to comply without losing face
Know the policy on physical intervention and that it is a last resort requiring training
Restore afterwards: reconnect with the student rather than leaving the incident hanging
strong_answer_signals: Prevention and routines before response
Low key responses first
Restores the relationship afterwards
avoid: Public confrontation
Any physical handling without training and policy
Applying a different standard from the teacher

questions.text: What do you know about individual education plans and targets?

key_points: Know what the plan is: the student needs, the agreed targets, the strategies, and the provision that must be delivered
Read it before working with the student rather than learning by trial and error
Deliver the strategies as written. Consistency across adults is most of what makes a plan work
Record against the targets: what was done, what the student achieved, and how much support was needed
Feed observations back. You often see things in the moment that a teacher or specialist cannot
Attend or contribute to reviews where you are included, since your evidence is the most detailed available
Know that a plan may be legally binding provision, not a suggestion
strong_answer_signals: Reads the plan before working with the student
Records against targets with the support level
Understands the provision may be legally required
avoid: Working from what you think is best instead of the plan
Not recording anything
Treating targets as background information

questions.text: How do you support a student with a specific learning difficulty?

key_points: Say what you know about the profile: dyslexia, dyscalculia, dyspraxia, ADHD, autism, speech and language needs
Match the support to the barrier rather than the label. Two students with the same diagnosis need different things
Practical strategies: chunking, visual supports, overlays or fonts, pre teaching vocabulary, task boards, timers, movement breaks, reduced writing demand
Use the technology where available: text to speech, speech to text, recording, and word prediction
Protect self esteem. Support that marks a student out publicly costs more than it gains
Say that you follow the specialist advice from the school rather than internet strategies
strong_answer_signals: Supports the barrier rather than the label
Names practical strategies
Follows specialist advice
avoid: Treating a diagnosis as a fixed recipe
Making the support visible in a way that embarrasses the student
Using strategies you found online instead of the plan

questions.text: How do you record and report on student progress?

key_points: Record what was actually done and what the student produced, with the level of support needed
Be specific and factual. Completed six of ten questions with verbal prompts is useful, tried hard is not
Record behaviour incidents factually and without interpretation. Describe what happened, not why you think it happened
Keep records securely. This is personal data about children and it has the same protection as any other
Feed back to the teacher the same day where it matters, not at the end of the week
Say how your notes help the teacher plan the next lesson
strong_answer_signals: Records support level, not just completion
Factual rather than interpretive
Same day feedback on what matters
avoid: Vague notes like worked well today
Interpreting motive in a behaviour record
Leaving student records where others can see them

questions.text: How do you run a small group intervention?

key_points: Know the programme and follow it as designed. Interventions work because they are delivered as intended
Prepare before the session: resources ready, the space set up, and knowing where each student left off
Keep the pace and the routine consistent. Students in intervention groups usually need predictability most
Manage the group so one student does not absorb all the time
Assess as you go and record it, since the point of an intervention is measurable progress
Feed back to the teacher and flag when a student is not responding, so the provision can change
Return the student to class in a way that does not draw attention
strong_answer_signals: Delivers the programme as designed
Records measurable progress
Flags when it is not working
avoid: Improvising the intervention content
Running it without recording outcomes
Letting a group become a chat

questions.text: What do you know about health, safety and personal care in a school?

key_points: Know the basics: fire procedure, first aid arrangements, medical plans, allergies and epipen location, and the risk assessments for your activities
Follow medical protocols exactly. Never give medication outside the agreed procedure
Personal care: follow the agreed care plan, protect dignity and privacy, follow the policy on who is present, and record it
Supervision: know your ratios on trips and in the playground, and never let supervision lapse because you are talking to a colleague
Report accidents and near misses through the school system
Say that you check for allergies and medical needs before any food related activity
strong_answer_signals: Knows medical protocols are followed exactly
Protects dignity in personal care and records it
Checks allergies before food activities
avoid: Giving medication informally
Personal care outside the agreed plan or without a record
Supervision lapses during playground duty

questions.text: How do you support learning in a specific subject?

key_points: Be honest about your subject confidence. Employers would rather know than discover it during a lesson
Prepare: read the lesson plan, and check you understand the content and the method the teacher uses before the lesson
Use the school method, not the one you were taught. Different subtraction methods confuse students badly
Ask the teacher when you are unsure rather than guessing in front of the student
For reading: hear the student read, support decoding, check comprehension, and record fluency
For maths: use concrete materials before abstract, and check understanding rather than answers
strong_answer_signals: Honest about subject confidence
Uses the school method
Asks rather than guessing in front of a student
avoid: Teaching a different method from the teacher
Guessing at content in front of the class
Not reading the lesson plan

questions.text: How do you promote independence in the students you support?

key_points: This is the professional test of the role. A student who cannot function without their assistant has been failed, not helped
Fade prompting deliberately and record the level. The plan should move towards less support, not more
Teach the strategy rather than the answer: how to find it, how to check it, how to ask for help appropriately
Encourage peer support so the adult is not the only route
Step back physically. Sitting beside a student all lesson creates dependence and it also marks them out
Celebrate independent work specifically so the student notices the progress too
strong_answer_signals: Frames dependence as a failure of support
Fades prompting with a record
Uses peer support to reduce adult reliance
avoid: Being permanently attached to one student
Measuring success by how much you helped
Doing the task so the work looks finished

questions.text: How do you handle confidentiality in a school?

key_points: Everything about a child stays within the professional circle: the teacher, the relevant staff, and the safeguarding lead
Do not discuss students in corridors, staff rooms where others can hear, or at the school gate
Never discuss one child with another child parent, however casual the question
No social media contact with students or families, and no photographs on personal devices
Records and plans stay secure and are not taken home unless the policy allows
The exception is safeguarding. A concern is shared upward regardless of who asked you to keep it quiet
strong_answer_signals: Knows safeguarding overrides confidentiality
No social media or personal device photographs
Careful about corridor and gate conversations
avoid: Discussing a child with another parent
Taking photographs on a personal phone
Keeping a safeguarding concern quiet because a parent asked

questions.text: What makes a classroom routine work?

key_points: Consistency between adults. Students test the boundary with whoever is least consistent, and that is usually the person who has not been briefed
Clear routines for the moments that break down: entry, transitions, getting equipment, tidying, lining up, and leaving
Prepare the environment: resources ready, seating as planned, visual timetable visible where used
Know the signals the teacher uses and use the same ones
Anticipate the friction points and be positioned where they happen rather than at the front
Transitions are where most learning time is lost. Say that, because it shows you have actually watched a classroom
strong_answer_signals: Names consistency between adults as the key
Knows transitions lose the most time
Positions themselves at the friction points
avoid: Using your own signals and rules
Standing at the front rather than where support is needed
Only supporting during the main task, not transitions

questions.text: A student refuses to do the work. What do you do?

key_points: Stay calm and do not make it a public battle. A refusal in front of an audience becomes about pride
Find the reason quietly: too hard, too much writing, does not understand, tired, upset about something else, or avoidance of failure
Reduce the barrier rather than the expectation where you can: chunk it, scribe part, start it together, change the format
Offer a limited choice so the student keeps some control: this question or that one, now or in two minutes
Follow the plan or the school policy if refusal is a known pattern
Tell the teacher, because a pattern of refusal is information about the work as much as the student
strong_answer_signals: Looks for the reason before responding
Reduces the barrier rather than lowering expectations
Offers a limited choice
avoid: A public standoff
Doing the work to get it finished
Not telling the teacher about a pattern

questions.text: A student tells you something that worries you. What do you do?

key_points: Listen. Do not interrupt, do not lead, and do not ask probing questions
Never promise to keep it secret. Say that you may need to tell someone whose job it is to help
Reassure them that telling you was the right thing to do
Record it as soon as possible in their own words, with the date, time and context
Report to the designated safeguarding lead immediately. Not at the end of the day, and not after you have decided how serious it is
Do not investigate, do not tell other staff who do not need to know, and do not discuss it with the family
strong_answer_signals: Reports immediately without filtering
Never promises secrecy
Records in the child own words
avoid: Waiting until the end of the day
Asking questions to find out more
Deciding it is probably nothing

questions.text: A student becomes physically aggressive. What do you do?

key_points: Safety first: protect the other students, move them away rather than moving the student where possible
Stay calm and low key. A raised voice escalates it
Use the de-escalation strategies in the plan: space, quiet, choices, a known calming activity
Only use physical intervention if you are trained and the policy permits it, and only as a last resort to prevent harm
Get help. Send for the trained staff or the lead rather than managing alone
Afterwards: record it factually, follow the reporting procedure, and take part in the review of what triggered it
Reconnect with the student later. The relationship matters more than the incident
strong_answer_signals: Moves the audience rather than the student
Only trained physical intervention, as a last resort
Reconnects afterwards
avoid: Untrained restraint
Raising your voice or squaring up
Handling it alone rather than getting help

questions.text: You disagree with how a teacher is handling a student. What do you do?

key_points: Never contradict them in front of students. That undermines both of you and the students notice immediately
Raise it privately and at a good moment, framed around the student rather than the teacher judgement
Bring what you have observed, since your view from beside the student is genuinely different from theirs at the front
Ask rather than tell: I noticed X, would it help if I tried Y
Accept the teacher decision. They hold the responsibility for the class
Escalate only if it is a safeguarding or a safety issue, and then through the proper route without delay
strong_answer_signals: Raises it privately and frames it around the student
Offers observations rather than judgements
Escalates safeguarding immediately
avoid: Contradicting a teacher in the room
Going straight to the head without speaking to the teacher
Staying silent about a safeguarding concern to keep the peace

questions.text: You are asked to cover a class alone. What do you do?

key_points: Check what the school policy allows. In many places a teaching assistant covering a class has specific limits
Ask for the plan and the register, and confirm who to call if something happens
Keep the routine steady. Students respond to the routine more than to the adult
Deliver the work set rather than improvising a lesson, and keep the students working
Manage behaviour with the school system, and get support early rather than late
Report back to the teacher on what was covered and anything that happened
strong_answer_signals: Checks the policy limits
Asks for the plan and the escalation contact
Keeps routine and delivers the set work
avoid: Improvising a lesson with no plan
Not knowing who to call
Letting the routine collapse

questions.text: Two students are arguing and it is escalating. What do you do?

key_points: Intervene early and calmly, before it becomes physical. Presence alone often stops it
Separate them and give each some space rather than demanding an immediate explanation
Hear each side separately once they are calm. Trying to resolve it while both are angry does not work
Focus on the behaviour and what needs to happen next rather than on who started it
Follow the school system for consequences, and involve the teacher or the lead
Restore the relationship where you can, since these students still have to work together tomorrow
strong_answer_signals: Intervenes early with presence
Separates before questioning
Restores rather than only punishing
avoid: Trying to establish blame in the middle of it
Letting it run to see if they sort it out
Physically pulling students apart when untrained

questions.text: The student you support is absent. What do you do?

key_points: Ask the teacher what would help most rather than waiting to be told
Options that are genuinely useful: support another student or group, prepare resources, catch up on recording, run an intervention, prepare for the student return
Use the time to read the plans and the notes you never get to during a normal week
Say that you never treat it as a day off, since that is exactly what this question is testing
Prepare something for the student return so they can catch up
strong_answer_signals: Asks the teacher rather than waiting
Uses the time productively
Prepares for the student return
avoid: Treating it as free time
Waiting to be given a job
Sitting in the staff room

questions.text: A parent stops you and asks how their child is doing. What do you do?

key_points: Be warm and give the general, factual, day level answer: they had a good morning, they enjoyed the science activity
Do not give assessment information, behaviour judgements, comparisons with other children, or anything about a diagnosis
Direct anything substantive to the teacher, and offer to pass on that they would like a conversation
Never discuss another child
Report the conversation to the teacher, especially if the parent raised a concern
Say that this boundary protects the parent as much as the school, since they should get the full picture from the teacher
strong_answer_signals: Warm but stays within the boundary
Passes the request to the teacher
Reports concerns raised informally
avoid: Giving progress or behaviour details
Comparing their child to others
Not telling the teacher a concern was raised

questions.text: You notice a student is being excluded or bullied.

key_points: Do not ignore it and do not wait to be certain. Low level exclusion is where bullying starts
Intervene in the moment in a way that does not spotlight the student: change a grouping, join the activity, redirect the group
Talk to the student privately and gently. Ask open questions rather than telling them what is happening
Report it to the teacher and follow the school anti bullying policy. Passing it on is required, not optional
Record what you observed factually with dates, since a pattern is what gets acted on
Follow up. Checking again next week is what tells you whether anything changed
strong_answer_signals: Acts on low level exclusion rather than waiting for proof
Intervenes without spotlighting
Records with dates so a pattern is visible
avoid: Waiting to be sure before reporting
Confronting the group publicly
Reporting once and never following up

questions.text: You are given more students to support than you can manage.

key_points: Say what is possible with the numbers you have, and ask the teacher to set the priority
Focus where the support is required rather than where it is easiest. A student with a legally required provision comes first
Use grouping so you are supporting several students at once rather than one at a time
Raise it properly if it is a persistent pattern, with specifics about the students and the provision that is not being delivered
Record accurately what was delivered. If required provision is not happening, that record is what changes it
Never quietly absorb it, because the students who lose out are the ones who cannot speak up
strong_answer_signals: Asks the teacher to set the priority
Protects legally required provision first
Records what was not delivered
avoid: Spreading thinly so nobody gets real support
Silently absorbing an impossible allocation
Prioritising the easiest students

questions.text: How do you deploy and lead a team of teaching assistants?

key_points: Deploy by need and by provision rather than by habit. The most experienced assistant should usually be with the highest need, not the easiest class
Make sure every assistant knows the plan for their students and has read it
Build in briefing time with teachers. Assistants deployed with no briefing are the single biggest waste in a school
Timetable the interventions properly rather than fitting them in around gaps
Observe and coach, and give feedback that is specific and about the student outcome
Track the impact: are the students they support making progress, and can you show it
strong_answer_signals: Deploys by need rather than habit
Protects briefing time with teachers
Tracks student outcomes, not activity
avoid: Deploying by who gets on with whom
No briefing time built into the timetable
Measuring assistants by how busy they look

questions.text: How do you evidence the impact of support staff?

key_points: Start from the student outcomes: progress against targets, independence levels, attendance, behaviour incidents, reading or maths measures
Record support levels so a reduction in prompting is visible as progress
Use intervention entry and exit data rather than impressions
Compare against what would be expected without the support where you reasonably can
Be honest about what is not working. An intervention with no impact should be stopped rather than continued
Present it in the language a leadership team and an inspection use
strong_answer_signals: Measures independence, not just attainment
Uses entry and exit data
Stops interventions that show no impact
avoid: Evidencing activity rather than outcomes
Continuing an intervention because it has always run
No baseline to compare against

questions.text: How do you handle a support staff member who is not following a plan?

key_points: Check the plan is clear and that they have actually been given it and trained on it. Very often they have not
Observe rather than relying on report, and give specific feedback about what you saw
Diagnose the cause: unclear expectations, disagreement with the approach, workload, confidence, or a relationship with the student
Model it or arrange for them to watch someone doing it well
Set a clear expectation with a review date and keep it
Follow the formal process if it does not improve, but only after real support
Act quickly where the issue affects a student safety or a legal provision
strong_answer_signals: Checks they were actually trained on the plan
Observes rather than relying on report
Acts fast where provision is legally required
avoid: Assuming non compliance is defiance
Feedback with no modelling or support
Letting a provision breach continue while a process runs

questions.text: How do you support inclusion across a school?

key_points: Quality first teaching comes before intervention. Most inclusion is won in the classroom, not in a separate room
Support teachers to adapt: modelling, resources, planning support, and training on the most common needs
Watch for support that segregates. A student permanently outside the classroom with an adult is not included
Involve students and families in the plan rather than designing it around them
Track who is being withdrawn, how often, and whether it is working
Build the culture: language, expectations, and staff confidence with additional needs
strong_answer_signals: Quality first teaching before intervention
Watches for support that segregates
Tracks withdrawal patterns
avoid: Solving inclusion by allocating more adults
Withdrawing students without reviewing the impact
Designing provision without the family

questions.text: How do you manage safeguarding as a leader?

key_points: Everyone trained, at induction and refreshed, including temporary and volunteer staff
Make the reporting route unmissable: who the lead is, how to report, and that reporting is always right
Record and monitor patterns rather than treating each concern as isolated. The pattern is usually the case
Act on low level concerns about adults too, since that is where most serious cases were missed
Never let a concern wait for more evidence, and never allow a culture where reporting feels disloyal
Audit yourself: check the records, check the follow ups, check that referrals were actually made
strong_answer_signals: Trains temporary staff and volunteers too
Monitors patterns rather than isolated incidents
Acts on low level concerns about adults
avoid: A reporting route only permanent staff know
Waiting for more evidence before referring
Treating a concern about a colleague differently

questions.text: How do you handle a difficult conversation with a family?

key_points: Prepare: know the facts, the history, and what you can actually offer before the meeting
Start from the shared goal, which is always the child
Be honest and specific rather than softening until the message disappears. Families usually already know
Listen properly. A parent who feels blamed stops hearing anything else
Bring options and next steps rather than only a problem, and agree who does what by when
Record it and follow up in writing so there is no ambiguity
Involve the right people: the teacher, the special needs coordinator, or external services
strong_answer_signals: Honest without softening the message away
Brings options and agreed next steps
Follows up in writing
avoid: Softening until the message is lost
Blaming the family
No written record of what was agreed

questions.text: How do you develop support staff?

key_points: Find out what they actually need rather than sending everyone on the same course
The highest value training is usually specific: a particular need, a behaviour approach, an intervention programme, or subject knowledge
Use the people you have: peer observation, modelling, and pairing a new assistant with a strong one
Give real responsibility: leading an intervention, mentoring, contributing to reviews
Include support staff in meetings and training that affect the students they work with. Excluding them is common and it shows
Recognise the work publicly. Support staff are the most likely to feel invisible in a school
strong_answer_signals: Targets training rather than blanket courses
Includes support staff in relevant meetings
Gives real responsibility
avoid: Training days that are the same for everyone
Excluding assistants from planning about their own students
Development that never leads to responsibility

questions.text: How do you allocate a limited support budget?

key_points: Start from statutory and legally required provision. That is not optional and it is funded first
Then highest need and greatest impact, evidenced rather than assumed
Consider whether an adult is the right answer. Sometimes technology, a resource, or teacher training delivers more per pound
Avoid spreading so thin that nothing works. Partial provision often achieves nothing at all
Be transparent with staff and families about how decisions are made, since the perception of fairness matters
Review the impact and be willing to move resource away from something that is not working
strong_answer_signals: Statutory provision first
Considers non staffing solutions
Refuses to spread so thin that nothing works
avoid: Allocating by who asks loudest
Assuming an adult is always the answer
Never reviewing whether the allocation worked

questions.text: Why do you want to work with children?

key_points: Give a real reason: seeing something click, the progress you can watch happen, the relationships, the variety of a school day
Connect it to something you have actually done, in work, volunteering, or family life
Say what age group you work best with and why
Be honest about practical reasons such as school hours, since employers know and respect it when paired with genuine interest
strong_answer_signals: A concrete reason tied to real experience
Knows which age group suits them
Honest about practical motivations
avoid: Saying you love children as the whole answer
Only mentioning the holidays and the hours
Nothing about learning or progress

questions.text: Why this school?

key_points: Show you have looked: the intake, the values, the inspection report, the specialist provision, the way they describe themselves
Say something specific that fits what you are good at, such as their approach to inclusion or a particular provision
Connect it to your experience with a similar community or need
Be honest about practical fit alongside the real reason
strong_answer_signals: Specific knowledge of the school
Connects their strengths to the school context
Honest about practical fit
avoid: An answer that fits any school
Getting the school phase or intake wrong
Only mentioning the location

questions.text: What makes a good teaching assistant?

key_points: Name the real qualities with evidence: patience, consistency, knowing when to step back, discretion, reliability, and noticing what others miss
Say that the hardest skill is not helping too much
Mention the professional side: following plans, recording accurately, and safeguarding
Say something about the relationship with the teacher, since half the job is that partnership
strong_answer_signals: Names not helping too much as the hard skill
Includes the professional and recording side
Values the teacher partnership
avoid: A list of adjectives
Only describing kindness
Nothing about safeguarding or plans

questions.text: Do you want to become a teacher?

key_points: Answer honestly. Both answers are fine and dishonesty is what causes a problem later
If yes: say so, say what you want to learn from this role, and commit to the time you will give
If no: say why this role suits you and that you value it as a career in its own right. Many of the best assistants never want to teach
Either way, make clear you intend to do this job properly rather than treating it as a waiting room
strong_answer_signals: Honest either way
Values the assistant role in its own right
Commits to doing the job properly regardless
avoid: Saying no when you mean yes
Treating the role as a stepping stone out loud
Being vague to avoid the question

questions.text: How do you handle the emotional side of this work?

key_points: Be honest. Working with children who have difficult circumstances is emotionally demanding and pretending otherwise is not credible
Say what you do: talking to the right people, using supervision or debriefs where they exist, keeping boundaries, and switching off
Say that boundaries protect the child too. Over involvement is not the same as care
Know when to ask for support, and say that you would
Mention the positive side honestly, since the progress is what sustains people in this work
strong_answer_signals: Honest about the emotional demand
Has real coping habits, not just resilience claims
Understands boundaries protect the child too
avoid: Claiming it never affects you
Over involvement described as commitment
No support strategy at all

questions.text: Do you have any questions for us?

key_points: Ask what tells you what the role really is:
"Which students would I be supporting, and would it be one to one or across a class?"
"How is time built in for briefing with the class teacher?"
"What training is provided, particularly for specific needs?"
"How are interventions timetabled and recorded?"
"Who is the designated safeguarding lead?"
Asking about teacher briefing time is the question that shows you have actually done this job
strong_answer_signals: Asks about briefing time with the teacher
Asks about training for specific needs
Asks who the safeguarding lead is
avoid: No questions
Only asking about hours and holidays
Asking something in the job description
